decisions.reason: The source says everyone sprang into action; SOL narrows this to animals scurrying for shelter.
“Settled inside caves” keeps the animals’ retreat and reads naturally.
SOL preserves the effort to keep warm against the relentless rain.
SOL combines this realization with the next sentence without dropping its meaning.
The rain’s unexpected protection is retained in H004.
“Felt as though” preserves the comparison that the entire grassland was trembling.
The animals’ bristling is retained in H008.
SOL keeps the animals’ bristling and sensory perception of what follows.
SOL preserves the dense rain and the riders crossing the land.
SOL makes the hooves drive onward and drops the horses’ forceful charge; the source has the horses charging ahead.
SOL drops that the lean man muttered, an explicit speech cue in the source.
The name identifies the man, so omitting the repeated description changes nothing.
The hoarse voice and furrowed brow are preserved in natural phrasing.
The gestures and approaching cavalry remain; the omitted “like the wind” is not essential to the action.
“Commander of a thousand” accurately renders the rank and remains clear.
Temur’s effort to sound stern is retained in H017.
SOL preserves the stern order and both khans’ names as the basis for punishment.
“Yes, sir!” is a natural affirmative response to the order.
The cavalrymen still salute and disperse in every direction.
“Swallowed dryly” preserves the source’s dry swallow; SOL drops that physical detail.
SOL drops the source’s tag question, “Right?” before “my proud brother.”
SOL clearly preserves the pat on Temur’s armor and his startle.
“You must be cold” preserves the concern expressed in the source.
“What’s in your heart” naturally conveys knowing Temur’s feelings.
The source says Chinggen suddenly clenched his teeth; SOL drops the sudden beat.
“Tear to pieces” preserves the threat without imposing the more specific “limb from limb.”
SOL drops Chinggen’s attribution and replaces the established term “killing intent” with “murderous eyes.”
“Everyone on the grasslands” preserves the scope of who knew.
“Each had brought” preserves that both men arrived at the meeting with retainers.
“Stained with blood” retains the image of the ger soon being bloodied.
“Plotting something so terrible” preserves the accusation without changing its meaning.
SOL preserves their origin in the Central Plains and their identification as Murim martial artists.
The retainers’ deaths in pools of blood remain clear and source-faithful.
SOL drops the source’s “in an instant,” which emphasizes how quickly the eastern grasslands could have fallen.
White knuckles naturally convey Chinggen gripping the reins tightly.
The source says they judged the two men would become a threat; SOL changes that prospective judgment to a present one.
“Cold look” preserves the hostile expression in Chinggen’s eyes.
SOL omits the source’s explicit agent “by them” from the claim that everyone was being used.
“Nodded as one” naturally conveys their simultaneous agreement.
“He was right” preserves the narration’s confirmation.
Naming the nomads clarifies the source’s referent without changing the claim.
“That had not changed” naturally refers back to the contempt described in context.
“Their contempt had become hatred” preserves the shift in attitude.
SOL drops the source’s “a mere band of” barbarians, which specifies the group as a small band.
SOL preserves the fading memory of ancestral achievements and the resulting desire for something new.
The contrast between peace and conquest is unchanged.
The contrast between wealth and horse manure is unchanged.
Naming Temur and Chinggen preserves the two young men’s identity without changing the welcome.
The names are already present in H048, so the separate repetition is unnecessary.
The source has Chinggen lament; “spoke bitterly” drops that explicit emotional action and adds bitterness.
SOL preserves the regret, the need to think more deeply, and the leader’s responsibility.
The calm, powerful voice and its arrival are preserved.
The source says the warriors will be embraced by Tengri; “rest in Tengri’s embrace” changes that image.
The man’s appearance and Chinggen’s widened eyes are preserved.
SOL drops Chinggen’s question about how Jamukha came all the way there.
“Cries rose” naturally conveys the greetings erupting around them.
SOL preserves the force in Jamukha’s gaze; the following dialogue makes the omitted “then spoke” redundant.
“Sideburns” accurately identifies the hair at his temples.
“Only how he looked” retains the contrast between Jamukha’s appearance and age.
SOL preserves Jamukha’s status and incorporates the following sentence about his army.
The number of tribespeople and Jamukha’s practical leadership are retained in H060.
SOL naturally expresses gratitude for being entrusted with the vanguard.
The source hedges that the Han Chinese probably did not know; SOL makes their ignorance categorical.
SOL preserves the admiration and reverence already directed at Jamukha.
“According to the story” naturally conveys what was known about the earlier attack.
Jamukha’s proven prowess is retained in H067.
SOL makes the massacre seem caused by the number of Han Chinese, whereas the source describes the battle itself as massacre-like.
The failed plot and Jamukha’s march toward the Central Plains are preserved.
“Just as he was doing now” retains the comparison to the present moment.
SOL drops that Jamukha answered calmly, an explicit manner of speaking in the source.
“A warrior who represented an entire tribe” preserves the comparison to a tribe’s representative warrior.
SOL preserves the army’s size and that its confidence rests on more than hope.
The questioning response about the Keshik is preserved.
“We would have asked you ourselves” accurately conveys that they would have made the request.
“Natural decision” preserves the sense that putting the strongest warriors first was to be expected.
The Sound Transmission and Jamukha’s moving lips remain; “in his ear” is a natural rendering.
SOL preserves the pointed reminder that Chinggen had just said they would ask Jamukha.
“That was…” preserves the speaker’s hesitation and unfinished response.
The source says they will cross in the shortest possible time; SOL’s “as quickly as possible” weakens that explicit superlative.
SOL removes the contemptuous image of the area crawling with expendable arrow-fodder.
The named figures, timing, and dismissive reference to Shanxi opponents are preserved.
“Stared straight at” preserves Jamukha’s direct gaze at the source of the transmission.
“Keep … under control” preserves the order to rein in the idiot.
“Kept the smarter one alive” faithfully conveys the suggestion to spare him.
SOL preserves the barely noticeable chuckle and the gesture over his face.
The speaker’s qualified praise and the attempt to negotiate amid his men’s deaths are preserved.
“Yielded” and “stood firm” preserve the contrast between Temur’s surrender and Chinggen’s mettle.
SOL drops “that much,” weakening the source’s explicit comparison that heartfelt surrender makes someone easier to handle.
The amused gaze still sweeps across the army filling the grasslands.
“A little more than a day’s travel” conveys the remaining distance of roughly a day.
“The walls” preserves the source’s unspecified fortress walls without adding a fortress.
